concept:
### Read a table like a detective

A club leader hands you a table of games and scores. Before you can answer anything about the club, you need to know what each row is about.

One row is a record. In this file a record describes a fictional player summary. A field is a column such as game or score. The player_id field lets you find the same player again even if two players have the same score.

CSV is a text format that stores a table. Pandas loads the CSV as a DataFrame, a table Python can work with. The starter calls that table df. Calling head() previews the first five records so you can check that the file loaded as expected.

### A table from file to screen

![A table with four field names and two player records. The P01 row is shaded.](../resources/diagrams/lesson01.png)

### Words to know

- **Record** — One row describing a single item or event.
- **Identifier** — A field used to recognise a record.

### Watch for this

A preview can show five records from a much larger file. Use shape when you need the size of the whole table.

head(2) requests two records. shape gives the row count followed by the column count. columns.tolist() gives the field names.

concept:
### Choose the numbers that answer the question

Imagine looking up the latest score on a scoreboard. You want the name and score columns. The other details can stay out of view.

Choose one column when you want to calculate with its values. Choose a list of column names when you want a smaller table. For example, df["score"] gives the score series. The inner brackets in df[["player_id", "score"]] hold the list of columns.

A summary reduces many values to a useful number. The minimum is the smallest value, the maximum is the largest and the mean is the sum divided by the number of values. Write the unit so the reader knows what the number measures.

### Three ways to summarise 8 12 and 16

![Minimum. 8 points. Mean. (8 + 12 + 16) ÷ 3. Maximum. 16 points](../resources/diagrams/lesson02.png)

### Words to know

- **Series** — A single Pandas column.
- **Mean** — Sum of the values divided by how many were used.

### Watch for this

max() reports the highest value. To identify the player who earned it, you also need the corresponding row.
worked:
Predict the result, then find or add these lines below the part of your starter that loads the data. Record your prediction and what happened in the pupil workbook.

```python
scores = df["score"]
print("Highest score", scores.max(), "points")
```

The first line displays a small table. The next two lines select a single series and reduce it to one value.

concept:
### Keep rows that pass a test

A club offers a badge to everyone scoring at least 80 points. You can turn the rule into a question with a True or False answer for each player.

A condition compares a value with a rule. Pandas checks the condition for every row and makes a Boolean mask, a list of True and False values lined up with the original rows. Applying the mask keeps the rows marked True.

A boundary is the point at which the rule changes. For “above 80” use > 80. For “at least 80” use >= 80, which includes 80. Use == to compare for equality, including when you compare a game name.

### The mask follows each row

![79 points. False · leave out. 80 points. True · keep. 81 points. True · keep](../resources/diagrams/lesson03.png)

### Words to know

- **Mask** — True or False values lined up with rows.
- **Boundary** — The value where the condition changes.

### Watch for this

Quote category names and match their spelling and capital letters. A blank result may mean the label did not match.
worked:
Predict the result, then find or add these lines below the part of your starter that loads the data. Record your prediction and what happened in the pupil workbook.

```python
mask = df["score"] > 80
selected = df[mask]
print(selected[["player_id", "score"]])
print("Matching rows", len(selected))
```

The condition builds the mask. The second line applies it. The last line counts the selected rows.

concept:
### Decide when both rules must pass

A quick-play challenge rewards a score of at least 80 and a session of at most 25 minutes. A player can meet either target on its own, or both.

AND keeps a row when both tests are True. OR keeps a row when at least one test is True, including rows that pass both. A truth table lets you test all four possible combinations before trying real data.

In a Pandas filter use & for AND and the vertical bar for OR. Put each comparison in parentheses so Python can combine the two masks correctly.

### Two tests for one player

![Score ≥ 80. Example score 82: True. Minutes ≤ 25. Example duration 30: False. AND or OR. AND rejects · OR keeps](../resources/diagrams/lesson04.png)

### Words to know

- **AND** — Both tests must pass.
- **OR** — At least one test must pass.

### Watch for this

Changing AND to OR can add rows. Compare the IDs so you can explain which rule each added row passes.
worked:
Predict the result, then find or add these lines below the part of your starter that loads the data. Record your prediction and what happened in the pupil workbook.

```python
high = df["score"] >= 80
short = df["minutes"] <= 25
print("Both", len(df[high & short]))
print("Either", len(df[high | short]))
```

The masks describe separate tests. Combine the masks and count the rows that survive each rule.

concept:
### Turn labels into evidence

A club wants to know whether one game appears more often than the others. Looking at a few players could give a different impression from checking every record.

A frequency is how often a category appears. value_counts() groups identical labels and counts them. Check the complete column when your question is about the full sample.

A percentage compares a count with a denominator. Divide the count by the total included in the calculation and multiply by 100. When you filter before counting, the denominator can change.

### From count to percentage

![Example count. 3 players. Example total. 12 players. Share. 3 ÷ 12 × 100 = 25%](../resources/diagrams/lesson05.png)

### Words to know

- **Frequency** — Number of times a value occurs.
- **Denominator** — The total you divide by.

### Watch for this

Three percentages rounded to one decimal place may sum to 99.9%. Check the underlying counts before deciding that a record is missing.
worked:
Predict the result, then find or add these lines below the part of your starter that loads the data. Record your prediction and what happened in the pupil workbook.

```python
counts = df["game"].value_counts()
print(counts)
print(counts / counts.sum() * 100)
```

First count the labels. Dividing by the sum gives the fraction of counted records in each category. Multiplying by 100 gives percent.

concept:
### Agree the ranking rule before sorting

A scoreboard can list players by highest score. A speed challenge might put the shortest session first. The same players can appear in a different order depending on the question.

Sorting puts records in order using a field. Descending puts the largest number first. Ascending puts the smallest number first. Keep the identifier so a position in a list can be traced to a player.

A tie rule tells the reader what happens when two primary values are equal. A second sort field such as player_id gives a repeatable display order. It does not make one tied score higher than another.

### Two keys for a ranking

![Main key. Score descending. Tie rule. Player ID ascending. Preview. First five after sorting](../resources/diagrams/lesson06.png)

### Words to know

- **Ascending** — Smallest first for numbers.
- **Tie rule** — A repeatable way to order equal primary values.

### Watch for this

head(5) returns the first five rows of the current table. Sort first if you mean the top five by a field.
worked:
Predict the result, then find or add these lines below the part of your starter that loads the data. Record your prediction and what happened in the pupil workbook.

```python

                        ascending=[False, True])
print(ranked[["player_id", "score"]].head(5))
```

Each True or False setting applies to the corresponding sort field. The printed table keeps the identity and the ranked value.

concept:
### Investigate a suspicious table

A volunteer copied club records into a new file. Some entries look odd. Before making a claim, work out which cells or records you can trust.

An audit is a record of problems you found, where you found them, and what you suggest doing. Different checks detect different faults. isna() finds missing values. duplicated() detects repeated rows. A type check can reveal text where you expected a number.

Keep the raw CSV so someone can repeat your checks. Record the affected identifier and the actual value. If you flag a negative duration, for example, record the ID and the value you saw.

### Choose a check for each problem

![Blank cell. Count missing values. Repeated record. Check duplicated rows. Number as text. Try numeric conversion](../resources/diagrams/lesson07.png)

### Words to know

- **Missing value** — An expected value that is absent.
- **Audit** — A record of checks and what they found.

### Watch for this

A repeated row and a repeated ID are different checks. A repeated ID with different values needs investigation before any decision to remove it.
worked:
Predict the result, then find or add these lines below the part of your starter that loads the data. Record your prediction and what happened in the pupil workbook.

```python
print(df.isna().sum())
print(df[df.duplicated(keep=False)])
numeric_scores = pd.to_numeric(df["score"], errors="coerce")
print(df[numeric_scores.isna()][["player_id", "score"]])
```

keep=False marks every copy of a repeated row. Conversion with errors="coerce" marks unconvertible values as missing in the temporary series.

concept:
### Make cleaning decisions repeatable

Suppose two pupils repair the same file in different ways and get different means. A written policy makes it possible to see which decision produced each answer.

In this lesson, remove exact duplicate rows, standardise game labels, convert the numeric fields, and mark negative durations as missing. Keep incomplete records in the main cleaned file. Save a separate CSV and keep the raw file for reruns.

An audit trail connects each change to an observed problem. Record before and after counts so another person can check the effect. You can compare the known-score mean with a mean after filling missing scores with the median as a sensitivity check.

### Keep the original and save a new version

![Raw CSV. Preserve as supplied. Cleaning policy. Apply repeatable rules. Clean CSV and log. Save both outputs](../resources/diagrams/lesson08.png)

### Words to know

- **Normalise** — Make equivalent values follow a common format.
- **Sensitivity check** — See how a result responds to a different choice.

### Watch for this

An estimated value changes a calculation. Label the estimate and keep track of which values were missing.
worked:
Predict the result, then find or add these lines below the part of your starter that loads the data. Record your prediction and what happened in the pupil workbook.

```python
clean = df.drop_duplicates().copy()
clean["game"] = clean["game"].str.strip().str.title()
print("Before", len(df), "after", len(clean))
```

The first line copies the deduplicated data into a separate table. The second trims outer spaces and standardises game labels.

concept:
### Make a category comparison easy to see

Imagine a club poster showing how many players chose each game. The reader should be able to tell what was counted and whether any game had more players.

A bar chart gives each category its own bar. Bar height represents the value. Start the vertical axis at zero for counts so the lengths show the sizes fairly. Give the chart a title that names the sample and label the vertical axis with what is counted.

Build the count table before plotting. Then check each bar against its count. A plain-language description should state the values and comparison so someone can read the result without seeing the chart.

### Read a bar from its baseline

![A bar chart showing Blue 2 players, Green 4 players and Gold 3 players, starting at zero.](../resources/diagrams/lesson09.png)

### Words to know

- **Baseline** — The starting level for a bar.
- **Category** — A named group such as a game.

### Watch for this

A chart title such as “Games” leaves out the question and sample. Tell the reader whose choices were counted.
worked:
Predict the result, then find or add these lines below the part of your starter that loads the data. Record your prediction and what happened in the pupil workbook.

```python
ax = counts.plot.bar(rot=15)
ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
```

The counts determine the heights. sort_index() puts the labels in order. The starter supplies the title, axis labels and save commands you will edit.

concept:
### Match the picture to the question

A club organiser wants to see how attendance changed over several weeks. Another wants to compare the numbers choosing different games. Each question calls for a different chart.

A line chart connects measurements in order and helps you see rises and falls over time. A bar chart compares categories. A scatter chart shows how two numeric values pair up for each record.

In the weekly file a row is a total for one week. Sort by week before drawing the line. The slope between two points represents the change between the measurements. The file gives no counts for the days in between.

### A line follows ordered measurements

![A line chart showing 6 visits in week 1, 9 in week 2 and 7 in week 3.](../resources/diagrams/lesson10.png)

### Words to know

- **Time series** — Measurements in time order.
- **Unit** — What a number is measured in.

### Watch for this

Visits can include return visits from the same person. Label the count as visits.
worked:
Predict the result, then find or add these lines below the part of your starter that loads the data. Record your prediction and what happened in the pupil workbook.

```python
ordered = df.sort_values("week")
ax = ordered.plot(x="week", y="visits",
                  kind="line", marker="o", legend=False)
```

Sorting makes the points join in week order. Each marker represents one measured weekly total.

concept:
### Read a cloud of points

A club coach wonders whether players who practise longer tend to earn higher scores. Each player contributes one pair of values, which can be plotted as one point.

A scatter plot places one numeric value on each axis. A point's horizontal position gives the practice minutes. Its vertical position gives the score in points. Look at the direction of the cloud, how widely it is spread, and points far from the general pattern.

An association is a pattern in how two recorded variables vary together. To judge a possible cause, you would need evidence about what happened first and other factors that could affect scores. A scatter plot of these reports can help you ask better questions.

### Every point is a pair of values

![A scatter plot of practice minutes and score. The point at 12 minutes and 55 points is labelled.](../resources/diagrams/lesson11.png)

### Words to know

- **Association** — A pattern connecting two recorded variables.
- **Scatter plot** — A chart with one point per paired observation.

### Watch for this

Even when the cloud tends upwards, two players with similar practice can have very different scores.
worked:
Predict the result, then find or add these lines below the part of your starter that loads the data. Record your prediction and what happened in the pupil workbook.

```python
ax.set(xlabel="Practice (minutes)", ylabel="Score (points)")
print(df[["player_id", "practice_minutes", "score"]].head())
```

The plot pairs values from the same row. The preview lets you check a point by reading the raw values next to its ID.

concept:
### Build a fair comparison between teams

A league organiser wants to compare teams and find ones meeting a performance target with limited training hours. Decide how to measure performance before ranking the teams.

Points per match is a derived field. Divide each team's points by the number of matches it played. In other datasets a team could have zero or missing matches, so check the denominator before calculating.

A regional average summarises the team rates in that region. Keep the count of teams alongside the mean. For the shortlist, test the points-per-match and training-hours conditions together.

### Turn totals into a rate

![Season points. 18 points. Matches played. 6 matches. Points per match. 18 ÷ 6 = 3](../resources/diagrams/lesson12.png)

### Words to know

- **Derived field** — A value calculated from existing fields.
- **Rate** — A quantity expressed per another quantity.

### Watch for this

A mean of team rates gives every team equal weight. Its interpretation can differ from dividing all points by all matches when teams play different numbers of matches.
worked:
Predict the result, then find or add these lines below the part of your starter that loads the data. Record your prediction and what happened in the pupil workbook.

```python
df["points_per_match"] = df["points"] / df["played"]
by_region = df.groupby("region")["points_per_match"]
print(by_region.agg(["count", "mean"]))
```

Division creates a value per row. groupby gathers teams by region, then agg shows how many rates went into each mean.

### Chart help

Take the mean from `by_region` and use `plot.bar()`. Reuse the title, axis and save steps from Lesson 9. Save your chart as `lesson12_sports.png`.

concept:
### Check what a chart makes you believe

Two posters use the same numbers. One makes a small difference look dramatic. Work out which design choice changes the impression.

A bar chart with a shortened vertical axis shows only part of each bar. The printed values can still be correct, while the visible lengths exaggerate the differences. Read the scale and compare the numerical values.

A very large value can also pull the mean upward. The median is the middle value of an ordered list and usually moves less when one value changes. Investigate an unusual value and explain any decision to keep or exclude it.

### Same values shown on different scales

![Two bar charts with 14 and 15 points. The second starts at 13, so the gap looks larger.](../resources/diagrams/lesson13.png)

### Words to know

- **Median** — The middle of an ordered set of values.
- **Truncated axis** — An axis that starts above its usual baseline.

### Watch for this

Check both the chart's scale and the calculation behind it. Changing one can alter the story in a different way from changing the other.
worked:
Predict the result, then find or add these lines below the part of your starter that loads the data. Record your prediction and what happened in the pupil workbook.

```python

print("Mean", example.mean())
print("Median", example.median())
```

The mean uses all five magnitudes. The median uses the middle position in the ordered list.

concept:
### Turn a mystery into an answerable question

A club has collected reports about a display glitch in fictional robots. Some reports mention an arcade visit. Start by finding out exactly what the reports record.

A row describes one robot report. flagged means a display glitch was reported, and clear means none was reported. The day field is the day of the report. No field gives the order of the visit and the glitch.

Before planning your analysis, check unique identifiers, missing fields and category values. Choose a question you can answer with the recorded fields. Name the groups and the measure you plan to compare.

### Plan the investigation

![Check the records. What does a row mean?. Choose groups. Which labels define them?. Choose a measure. What will you count or divide?](../resources/diagrams/lesson14.png)

### Words to know

- **Scope** — What your question covers.
- **Provenance** — Where the records came from and how they were made.

### Watch for this

A report can describe what was observed. To test what caused the glitch, you would need further evidence, such as visit and glitch times.
worked:
Predict the result, then find or add these lines below the part of your starter that loads the data. Record your prediction and what happened in the pupil workbook.

```python
print("Rows", len(df), "Unique IDs", df["robot_id"].nunique())
print(df.isna().sum())
print(df["status"].value_counts())
```

Comparing rows and unique IDs checks the one-report-per-robot assumption. The other lines inspect missingness and status labels.

concept:
### Compare groups using their own totals

A group with more flagged reports may simply have more robots. Compare both groups using a percentage that accounts for each group's size.

Count flagged reports within each group. Divide by the total reports in that same group and multiply by 100. Write both the fraction and percentage so readers can see the size of the group.

A Boolean column stores True for a flagged report and False for a clear report. In Pandas, sum counts the True values and count counts the non-missing entries. When each entry is present, the mean of the Boolean column is the flagged proportion.

### Compare two rates

![Dot diagrams show 6 of 10 flagged in group A and 8 of 20 in group B. The rates are 60% and 40%.](../resources/diagrams/lesson15.png)

### Words to know

- **Numerator** — The count above the fraction line.
- **Percentage point** — The unit for a difference between two percentages.

### Watch for this

Always check which total belongs under the fraction. Dividing every flagged count by the full file size answers a different question.
worked:
Predict the result, then find or add these lines below the part of your starter that loads the data. Record your prediction and what happened in the pupil workbook.

```python
df["is_flagged"] = df["status"] == "flagged"
groups = df.groupby("visited_arcade")["is_flagged"]
summary = groups.agg(["sum", "count", "mean"])
print(summary.assign(percent=summary["mean"] * 100))
```

The summary gives the flagged count, group total and flagged proportion for each visit category. The last line prints a percentage column.

concept:
### Check whether the pattern holds within groups

If visits and glitches both vary by area, an all-robot comparison may hide useful details. Repeat the comparison within each area to see what changes.

Grouping by area and reported arcade visit makes four subgroups. For each subgroup, record flagged count, total and percentage. Compare yes and no within Harbour, then yes and no within Hill.

A good evidence log records a finding, where it came from and what could limit it. Compare the within-area results with the combined result. Keeping group sizes visible lets the reader judge how much evidence sits behind each percentage.

### Split the comparison before making a claim

![All robots. Compare yes with no. Harbour only. Compare yes with no. Hill only. Compare yes with no](../resources/diagrams/lesson16.png)

### Words to know

- **Subgroup** — A smaller group inside the whole sample.
- **Alternative explanation** — Another reason a pattern could appear.

### Watch for this

In a group of ten, changing one report changes the percentage by ten points. Treat small subgroups with care.
worked:
Predict the result, then find or add these lines below the part of your starter that loads the data. Record your prediction and what happened in the pupil workbook.

```python
df["is_flagged"] = df["status"] == "flagged"
subgroups = df.groupby(["area", "visited_arcade"])
rates = subgroups["is_flagged"].agg(["sum", "count", "mean"])
print(rates.assign(percent=rates["mean"] * 100))
```

The list of grouping fields creates a row per area-and-visit combination. Read the denominator from the same row as its flagged count.

concept:
### Make a claim someone else can check

The club wants one useful answer from the fictional robot or team records. Choose a question that can be answered with the fields provided and build a short, repeatable analysis.

Start from an untouched CSV. Use a filter or group comparison and make at least two relevant calculations. Save a labelled chart and supporting table. Give field meanings and write one independent check of a value, boundary or denominator.

Draft a report that walks the reader from your question to the evidence and a cautious conclusion. State one limitation, give a text description of the chart and acknowledge any help. Use the report template in the pack for the final Markdown submission.

### An analysis another person can repeat

![Question and fields. Make the scope clear. Script and checks. Start with the raw file. Chart and report. Use evidence in your answer](../resources/diagrams/lesson17.png)

### Words to know

- **Verification** — An independent check of a result.
- **Reproduce** — Rerun the method and obtain the evidence again.

### Watch for this

A screenshot records what you saw. The script, raw CSV and saved evidence files let another pupil reproduce it.

concept:
### Defend your finding and improve it

Another pupil will try to follow your investigation and ask about a result. Use their questions to make your method clearer and your evidence easier to check.

Rerun your own Lesson 17 script from the raw data. Compare a generated output with the value in your report. If the values differ, locate the difference and record what you changed.

In a two-minute explanation, give the question, one finding with numbers and one limitation. Ask your partner for a specific suggestion. Make a justified revision and explain what it improves.

### Review with fresh evidence

![Rerun. Compare output with the report. Explain. Defend one result and its limits. Revise. Record the feedback and change](../resources/diagrams/lesson18.png)

### Words to know

- **Peer review** — Feedback from another pupil.
- **Revision** — A change you make after checking or receiving feedback.

### Watch for this

A partner can help you spot a problem. You should be able to explain your own code and predict what a small change would do.
